title: What changed for employers in Japan under the 2025 childcare and family care leave amendments?
description: Japan's 2025 Childcare and Family Care Leave Act changes: April and October 2025 notice, intention check and flexible work duties, and manager training.
shortAnswer: Japan's 2024 amendment to the Childcare and Family Care Leave Act took effect in two stages. From April 1, 2025, employers must individually inform and check the intentions of workers who report a family care need, give care information around age 40, and take care related measures such as training. From October 1, 2025, they must offer at least two flexible work options for children aged 3 to school age and hear and consider parents' intentions.
keyTakeaways: The amending law is Act No. 42 of 2024, promulgated May 31, 2024, with duties phased in on April 1, 2025 and October 1, 2025.
Article 21(4) and (5), from April 2025, require individual notice and intention confirmation when a worker reports a family care need, and care information in the period around age 40.
Article 22(4), from April 2025, requires at least one care related environment measure: training, a consultation desk, sharing in-house cases, or communicating a policy.
From October 2025, Article 23-3 requires two or more of five flexible work measures for parents of children aged 3 to school age, with individual notice before the child turns 3.
The MHLW circular says that where training is chosen, at least managers should have received it, and that notices must not discourage workers from using leave.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) and Prefectural Labor Bureau Equal Employment Departments
appliesTo: All employers in Japan, regardless of size, for the individual notice, intention confirmation and environment measures
Employers with more than 300 regular employees, for annual publication of childcare leave uptake from April 1, 2025
Line managers who receive pregnancy, childbirth or family care reports from workers
HR teams that run the individual notice and intention meetings
Workers raising children up to school age or caring for family members

sections.heading: Which law changed, and when did each stage take effect?

blocks.text: The changes come from Act No. 42 of 2024, which amended the Act on Childcare Leave, Caregiver Leave, and Other Measures for the Welfare of Workers Caring for Children or Other Family Members (Ikuji Kyūgyō, Kaigo Kyūgyō Tō Ikuji Mata wa Kazoku Kaigo o Okonau Rōdōsha no Fukushi ni Kansuru Hōritsu, Act No. 76 of 1991). It was promulgated on May 31, 2024. The MHLW [childcare and family care leave page](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/0000130583.html) publishes consolidated texts of the Act as at April 1, 2025 and as at October 1, 2025.

The [MHLW employer leaflet](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11900000/001259367.pdf) groups the changes into items 1 to 9 from April 1, 2025 and items 10 and 11 from October 1, 2025. As at November 2026, both stages are in force, and the [Act on e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/403AC0000000076) carries the amended articles cited on this page.

The April 2025 stage widened parental entitlements and created new duties to prevent people leaving work to care for family members. The leaflet lists nine items; the ones that change what managers and HR must do are below.

blocks.caption: Selected April 1, 2025 changes, from the MHLW leaflet

blocks.text: Under Article 21(4), when a worker tells the employer that a family member needs care, the employer must tell that worker individually about caregiver leave and other care support systems, where to apply, and caregiver leave benefits, and must check the worker's intentions. The method can be a meeting (online is allowed), a document, or fax or email if the worker wants that.

Under Article 21(5), the employer must give the same information to every worker within a set period: either the fiscal year in which the worker turns 40, or the year starting on their 40th birthday. Article 21(6) prohibits dismissal or other unfavorable treatment for making a report or because of the intentions expressed.

The October 2025 stage requires employers to offer flexible ways of working for parents of children aged 3 up to school age, and to hear and take into account parents' wishes at two points. These are items 10 and 11 in the MHLW leaflet.

Article 23-3(1) requires the employer to put in place two or more of five measures, and the worker chooses one. The five are: changes to start and finish times (flextime or staggered hours); telework available at least 10 days a month; running or arranging childcare facilities; a special leave of at least 10 days a year; and a short working hours system that includes a 6 hour day. Before choosing, the employer must hear the views of the majority union or worker representative under Article 23-3(4).

Article 23-3(5) requires the employer to notify each worker with a child under 3, individually and within the year before the child turns 3, of the measures it has chosen and where to apply, and to check the worker's intentions. Article 21(2) and (3), applied to that same window by Article 23-3(6), also require the employer to hear the worker's wishes about working hours, workplace, the period of using support systems and other conditions when the worker reports a pregnancy or birth, and to take those wishes into account.

sections.heading: Is training mandatory under the amended Act?

blocks.text: Training is one of several options rather than a stand-alone duty. Article 22(1) and (2) already required employers to take at least one measure to make childcare leave and caregiver leave requests easier, and from April 2025 Article 22(4) adds the same choice for other care support systems. In each case the options are training on the system, a consultation desk, or another measure set by ordinance.

The ordinance options are collecting and sharing in-house examples of workers who used the system, and communicating the system together with the employer's policy promoting its use. The guideline states that it is desirable to take more than one measure, and the MHLW leaflet repeats that advice for the care measures.

Where an employer chooses training, the MHLW [enforcement circular](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11900000/001378914.pdf) sets the expected scope: training should ideally cover every employee, "but at least managers should be in a state of having received the training" (translated). It says effective methods include running training regularly, basing it on surveys of the workplace, and dividing it by job grade with managers at the center. The circular applies this standard to childcare leave, caregiver leave and the new care support training alike.

sections.heading: What do the amendments mean for line managers?

blocks.text: Managers are usually the first people to hear about a pregnancy or a care situation, so they trigger the individual notice duties even when HR runs the meetings. A manager who does not pass the report on, or who responds in a way that discourages leave, can put the employer in breach.

items: The leaflet states that individual notice and intention confirmation designed to discourage workers from using the systems is not acceptable. Managers need to know what not to say.
Article 21(6) and Article 23-3(7) ban unfavorable treatment because of a report or the intentions a worker expresses. Workload, appraisal and allocation decisions after a report are exposure points.
Article 25 requires employers to prevent harassment related to the use of childcare and care systems, so managers' own comments matter.

Article 21(3) requires the employer to take the worker's stated wishes into account. The leaflet gives examples: adjusting working hours or location, reviewing workload, and revising working conditions.
The leaflet recommends periodic follow up meetings, for example on return from leave or while a worker uses short hours, to check that the chosen arrangement still fits.

blocks.text: For the broader harassment prevention framework managers already operate under, see [power harassment prevention obligations in Japan](/regulations/japan-power-harassment-prevention-obligations).

sections.heading: What happens if an employer does not comply?

blocks.text: The Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare can request reports and give advice, guidance or recommendations under Article 56. Under Article 56-2, if an employer does not follow a recommendation about listed duties, which include Article 21, Article 22(1), (2) and (4), and Article 23-3, the Minister can publish that fact.

Article 66 imposes a non-penal administrative fine of up to 200,000 yen on an employer that fails to report or reports falsely when asked under Article 56. These powers are exercised in practice by Prefectural Labor Bureaus.

sections.heading: How should an employer build training for the amended Act?

items: Brief every manager on what counts as a pregnancy, birth or care report and how to pass it to HR the same day.
Train HR staff who run notice meetings on the content required by Articles 21(4), 21(5) and 23-3(5) and on neutral, non discouraging wording.
Use the MHLW sample forms for individual notice and intention confirmation, adapted to your own systems.
Include scenarios on unfavorable treatment and harassment after a report.
Record completion by job grade so you can show that, at minimum, all managers have been trained.
Review the content whenever work rules change, and schedule refreshers using [mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

blocks.text: [How to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) cover how to structure the assignments and records.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry holds the April 2025 and October 2025 duties as separate dated obligations, each linked to the manager or HR role that triggers it and to the circular's expectation that managers are trained. Learning outcomes carry assessment points, such as identifying a care report in a scenario, so the record shows understanding as well as attendance.

faqs.q: Do small employers have to comply with the 2025 amendments?
faqs.a: Yes. The MHLW leaflet states that all items other than item 5, the publication of childcare leave uptake, apply to all companies. Publication applies only to employers with more than 300 regular employees. Small employers still need the notice, intention confirmation, environment and flexible work measures.

faqs.q: Can the individual notice be sent by email?
faqs.a: Yes, but only if the worker wants it. The leaflet lists four methods: a meeting, which may be online; handing over a document; fax; or email. Fax and email can be used only where the worker requests them. A meeting allows the employer to check intentions directly.

faqs.q: Does training on childcare leave count for the new care measure?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Article 22(4) covers care support systems such as caregiver leave days, overtime limits and short hours for care, separately from childcare leave under Article 22(1). Training can cover both, but its content must address the care systems for it to count toward Article 22(4).

faqs.q: Is the telework duty for parents of under 3s mandatory?
faqs.a: No. The April 2025 telework provisions for parents of children under 3 and for workers caring for family members are effort duties. By contrast, telework of at least 10 days a month is one of the five options an employer can choose to meet the mandatory Article 23-3 duty from October 2025.

Article 22(1), (2), (4): training, consultation system or other ordinance measure for childcare leave, caregiver leave and care support systems. Article 22-2: employers over 300 publish uptake annually. Article 23-3: two or more of five measures for children 3 to school age, hearing majority representative, individual notice before age 3, no unfavorable treatment. Article 25 harassment measures
